prize_parts.citation: For a poetic and essayistic oeuvre that renews lyric, verse narrative and elegy through a learned and emotionally charged encounter with antiquity, in which scholarship, translation and the shaping of the book become part of one imaginative practice.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Anne Carson as sole laureate. I changed only the citation scope. The standard I apply to 'sustained quality across the oeuvre' is whether a writer's central works carry human and imaginative depth through their form, and whether later work extends that form or only repeats it. I read the 'ideal direction' in Nobel's will as seriousness and depth of imaginative purpose, not as a rule about subject matter or an exclusion of learned or experimental work. Applied to Carson, Autobiography of Red turns the Stesichorus material into a verse novel about desire and difference. Nox turns the translation of Catullus 101, archival fragments and an address to a dead brother into an elegy. In both, the formal invention carries the feeling. The essays, the verse collections and the engagement with Greek texts share one recognisable voice and one method, so I read the body of work as a single practice. I do not treat it as a poet with a scholarly sideline. Applied to Cărtărescu, the same standard asks whether a large single cosmology keeps deepening. His voice and scale are exceptional and I do not rank the achievement lower. But I cannot test the deepening claim in Romanian, and I weigh repeated formal renewal across books above scale of construction. That is a judgment of weighting, not of talent. Because Carlberg and Sward argued that the citation must be bounded, I have drawn it from the established core of original poetry, verse narrative, elegy and essay. I name translation as part of the same practice and not as independent creation. I have dropped 'the book itself' from my round 1 wording, because the book-object dimension is the part a committee reading in translation or standard editions assesses least reliably.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which I cannot dismiss, is that Carson's effect depends partly on typography, layout, book design and a close relation to Greek and Latin originals. Some of this may be lost in Swedish or other translation, so the committee may be judging a partial image of the work. Her corpus is also more fragmentary than a novelist's, and the weight falls on a handful of books, above all Autobiography of Red and Nox. Colleagues have also raised, and I share, the worry that formal radicalism and erudition can be mistaken for sustained depth, and that some later and more occasional work may be mannered. The hybrid mode may also fit the 'ideal direction' less comfortably than Cărtărescu's larger imaginative project does. If members who have read the later books closely found that they only repeat the early gestures, my ordering between Carson and Cărtărescu would need to be reopened. I have no way inside this stage to settle that and do not claim to.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg prefers Cărtărescu for a single sensibility and a continuous project from the poetry through the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid. He worries that Carson's case rests on a stable core of acknowledged texts rather than continuous development, and he applies my 'ideal direction' question to both candidates.
responses.response: I accept that the question cuts both ways and I have applied one standard to both. One correction: in round 1 I listed Cărtărescu's translation dependence and my partial coverage of his poetry and early work as uncertainties. I did not argue that his length itself counts against him. On your concern about a stable core, I agree that this is the live risk for Carson. My answer is that her central books differ markedly in form from one another, and that is development, but I cannot verify the later books and you may be right that a citation should rest on the core. That is why I have bounded the citation to the established works. Your point that the claim for Cărtărescu also depends on testing specific volumes is one I share. Neither of us should treat his continuity or her renewal as established until it is tested. I would not use my own limit on Romanian against him.

responses.point: Mattson prefers Cărtărescu for a voice found nowhere else and for late novels that she says do not repeat the earlier ones. She also notes that bulk cannot count for him unless the books develop, and she doubts whether Carson's translations and book-object works belong to the core achievement.
responses.response: Your principle that bulk is not merit, and that the books must develop, is the one I apply to Carson as well. On the core, I have narrowed the citation so that it does not depend on the translations or on the folded book-object. In Nox the translation of Catullus is the elegiac form itself, so I keep it as part of one practice, but the claim rests on the original verse, elegy and essays. Where we still differ is weighting. You prefer a single cosmology realised at novel scale, and I prefer repeated invention of new forms. I cannot show that your reading of the late novels is wrong, and my coverage of his poetry and early work is thinner than I would like. If the committee can test those volumes in additional translations, your claim would be better supported than I can currently judge. I would then want the same test applied to Carson's later books.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Carson first, says that the later output may not match the peak of roughly 1998-2010, and argues that the will's 'ideal direction' should not be read as excluding learned or experimental work. He sees the test as whether the formal invention gives the work imaginative and human depth.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the will and use the same test. It is why I rest the case on grief and desire in Nox and Autobiography of Red and not on learnedness. Your point about the later output is the most useful qualification, and I now treat it as binding on drafting. The citation should be drawn from the established core and should not claim that recent work equals it. I would add that your own caution about economy in Cărtărescu is not a point against Carson alone, because it rests on the same question of control across a corpus. I would also not let my agreement with you stand in for argument. If the later books are mannered, that is a literary reason to move, and a count of colleagues who share my ranking is not.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson first but would keep the citation to the renewal of verse narrative, elegy and essay, drawn from the established core. She says she cannot fully discount mannerism and that the dependence on layout and book design remains a real limit.
responses.response: Your drafting advice has changed my citation. Following it, I name lyric, verse narrative and elegy and treat translation as part of the same practice. I removed the book itself from the claim, because we cannot judge it reliably. I share your view that this case is not settled, and I would not treat agreement among those who prefer Carson as evidence of her merit. We should also be explicit that Carson's supporters have not answered the question of whether the hybrid mode amounts to sustained depth or sometimes to erudite play. We have only said that the central books suggest the former. On Adonis, whom you and Olsson name as an alternative, I did not rank him in my opening and have not developed a case for him. I would need an argued literary case before I could weigh him.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson first and would anchor the case in original works: Eros the Bittersweet, Autobiography of Red, Plainwater, The Beauty of the Husband, Nox and later hybrid books. She treats the versions of Sappho and Greek drama as belonging to the same imaginative world without bearing the argument. She concedes that a closer reader could correct her on the later books.
responses.response: Your list of original works is the right basis for the citation, and I have used it. It lets the case survive even if a colleague gives translation little weight. I would qualify one thing. Naming original works does not answer the question about the later books, which you also concede you have not rechecked. That has to remain an open reservation, not something the citation assumes. I also agree that fragmentation is a method with a long lineage and not simply a gap in range. It should still be tested book by book, as you propose. If the committee found that only the 1990s and 2000s books carry the claim, the citation should say so and not use language implying continuous development.

uncertainties: I have not re-read the texts or independently verified any source. My view rests on public knowledge of the major books, especially Autobiography of Red and Nox.
How much of Carson's effect survives translation and standard editions is unresolved, given dependence on typography, layout and the relation to Greek and Latin originals.
Whether Carson's later and more occasional work keeps the level of the central books is unverified and is the main fact that could change my order.
Whether a hybrid, scholarly and fragmentary mode meets the 'ideal direction' of Nobel's will and the whole-oeuvre standard is a contested judgment, and I hold it as one.

My coverage of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose, poetry and early work is partial, and I cannot judge whether the late novels develop or repeat. The comparison between B004 and B028 is therefore unevenly informed.
I cannot judge Michon's French sentence texture through translation, and whether a compact corpus meets the whole-oeuvre standard is unresolved. I have developed no ranked case for Adonis.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the supplied profile, which records no personal, professional or family tie to Anne Carson, Mircea Cărtărescu or Pierre Michon. For context only, my own work includes ekphrasis, myth and fairy-tale motifs, and a Lagerlöf biography built on creative process, and these overlap thematically with parts of Carson's classical reworkings and with Michon's writing on art history. That is not a connection and is not evidence of a preference. My committee relations are limited to Swedish Academy colleagues, and my profile records no tie that bears on any shortlisted writer. My co-opted-then-full-member status is not documented as relevant. Disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
